reason: The wording holds, but the note cannot stay empty. I opened the Lascano PDF the verifier cites (strivingessences.com). It quotes “it is commonly believed that it is difficult to be happy, and there is much reason for such a belief; but it would be much easier for men to be happy if reflecting on and planning conduct preceded action” (DH 349), and its bibliography names the Bour and Zinsser Chicago volume, pp. 349 to 365. The quotation is lower-cased because it runs into her own sentence. That witness alone would not be enough: in May the same paper was shown to disagree with Lascano’s other paper over prejudice and prejudices on this very page. I found an independent third witness. The Diversity Reading List entry for Discourse on Happiness, 2009, Selected Philosophical and Scientific Writings, ed. Zinsser, trans. Bour and Zinsser, Chicago, pp. 349 to 365, reproduces the whole opening paragraph as its abstract. The sentence is capitalised there and word for word identical, and the paragraph goes on “One is carried along by circumstances and indulges in hopes that never yield half of what one expects.” So the capital It is attested and it is the opening sentence, which matches the French opening, On croit communément qu’il est difficile d’être heureux. The wording is therefore not a splice or a paraphrase. I still could not open the Chicago page: Google Books is quota-blocked, Internet Archive has no full text, and PhilPapers, Docsity and Medium return 403. This is the same state as May’s du Châtelet card, which ships hedged, and the Adrienne Rich carry, which ships verified with a note saying the Norton page was not opened. Consistency requires a plain note along the lines of: The Chicago volume was not opened; the wording agrees across three independent quotations of page 349, and all three agree on the opening sentence. Other checks: shipped.js shows it is not shipped and has no near match, du Châtelet is at 1 (month 5) and appears once in November, and she is not banned. The source line is about 118 characters, leads with the name, has no dash and names the translators and year. The Philosophy tag is right and the text is in scope (written in the 1740s, printed 1779). Editorially, as the verifier concedes, it has almost nothing to do with gratitude or mortality, so it should be the first to drop if the month is full.
